name: Ancient Rome
description: Questions covering: Kingdom and Republic, Roman Empire, Famous Commanders and Emperors, Roman Law and Culture, Fall of Rome. Test your knowledge.

questions.question: Who according to legend was the first king and founder of Rome in 753 BCE?
questions.explanation_correct: Romulus founded the city on the Palatine Hill and became its first ruler after killing his twin brother, Remus.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Remus died before the city was founded, Numa was the second king of Rome, and Aeneas was the Trojan ancestor of the Romans.

questions.question: What was the name of the highest advisory council in ancient Rome, composed of patricians, and later plebeians?
questions.explanation_correct: The Roman Senate (Senatus) controlled state finances, foreign policy, and advised magistrates during the republic.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Curia was a family division unit, the Centuriate Assembly decided on war, and the Tribunate represented the plebeians.

questions.question: How many consuls were elected annually during the Roman Republic to hold executive and military power?
questions.explanation_correct: Two consuls shared power and could veto each other's decisions to prevent the return of a monarchy.
questions.explanation_incorrect: One official was a dictator (only in crisis), three formed a triumvirate, and ten were decemvirs.

questions.question: Which Carthaginian general marched war elephants over the Alps and defeated the Romans at Cannae in 216 BCE?
questions.explanation_correct: Hannibal commanded Carthage's forces in the Second Punic War and dealt Rome its worst defeat at Cannae.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Hamilcar was Hannibal's father, Hasdrubal his brother, and Syphax a Numidian king allied with Carthage.

questions.question: Which Roman general defeated Hannibal at the Battle of Zama in 202 BCE, ending the Second Punic War?
questions.explanation_correct: Publius Cornelius Scipio was awarded the cognomen 'Africanus' for defeating Carthage on its own territory.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Marcellus fought in Italy, Fabius avoided pitched battles (hence 'Cunctator'), and Cato called for Carthage's destruction.

questions.question: Which Roman politician famously ended every speech in the senate with: 'Ceterum censeo Carthaginem esse delendam'?
questions.explanation_correct: Cato the Elder (Censor) saw Carthage's resurgence as a mortal threat, leading to the Third Punic War.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Cicero was an orator who fought Catiline, Caesar conquered Gaul, and Pompey was Caesar's rival.

questions.question: Which Thracian gladiator initiated the largest slave rebellion in Roman history in 73 BCE?
questions.explanation_correct: Spartacus escaped a gladiator school in Capua and led an army that resisted Roman legions for two years.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Crixus, Oenomaus, and Gannicus were his lieutenants and rebel commanders.

questions.question: Which three politicians formed the unofficial alliance known as the First Triumvirate in 60 BCE?
questions.explanation_correct: Julius Caesar, Pompey the Great, and Marcus Licinius Crassus combined their political, military, and financial influences.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Octavian, Antony, and Lepidus formed the Second Triumvirate, Sulla and Marius fought a civil war, and Brutus and Cassius killed Caesar.

questions.question: Crossing which river in 49 BCE did Julius Caesar initiate a civil war against Pompey?
questions.explanation_correct: The Rubicon was the boundary of Cisalpine Gaul. Crossing it with an army broke the law, prompting Caesar's 'Alea iacta est'.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Tiber flows through Rome, the Po is in northern Italy, and the Rhine bounded Germania.

questions.question: In which year BCE was Julius Caesar assassinated in the Theatre of Pompey by a group of senators on the Ides of March?
questions.explanation_correct: Conspirators led by Brutus and Cassius stabbed Caesar 23 times on March 15, 44 BCE.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 49 BCE was the start of the civil war, 31 BCE was the Battle of Actium, and 15 BCE was during Octavian's reign.

questions.question: In which naval battle in 31 BCE did Octavian defeat Mark Antony and Cleopatra, taking control of the empire?
questions.explanation_correct: The victory at Actium off Greece ended the civil wars and led to the creation of the empire.
questions.explanation_incorrect: At Pharsalus Caesar defeated Pompey, at Philippi Antony and Octavian beat Caesar's assassins, and at Mylae Rome beat Carthage at sea.

questions.question: Who was the first Roman Emperor, reigning from 27 BCE under the title 'Augustus'?
questions.explanation_correct: Gaius Octavius, Caesar's adopted son, created the system known as the Principate, keeping republican appearances while holding absolute power.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Caesar was never emperor, Tiberius was Augustus's successor, and Nero was the last of the Julio-Claudian dynasty.

questions.question: What was the name of the elite military unit created by Augustus to serve as the emperor's bodyguard and Rome's garrison?
questions.explanation_correct: The Praetorian Guard (Cohortes praetoriae) acquired massive political power, making and unmaking emperors.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Auxiliaries were non-citizen soldiers, vigiles were firefighters, and gladiators fought in arenas.

questions.question: Which Roman emperor of the Julio-Claudian dynasty famously persecuted Christians after the Great Fire of Rome in 64 CE?
questions.explanation_correct: Nero blamed the Christian sect for the fire, leading to cruel executions in his gardens.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Caligula was known for madness, Claudius conquered Britain, and Vespasian started the Colosseum.

questions.question: Which emperor of the Flavian dynasty ordered the construction of the Flavian Amphitheatre, known as the Colosseum?
questions.explanation_correct: Vespasian funded the Colosseum using spoils captured during the Jewish Revolt in Jerusalem.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Titus finished and opened it, Domitian expanded it, and Nero built his Golden House (Domus Aurea) nearby.

questions.question: Under which emperor of the Nerva-Antonine dynasty did the Roman Empire reach its maximum territorial expansion?
questions.explanation_correct: Trajan (reigned 98–117 CE) conquered Dacia, Arabia, and Mesopotamia, pushing borders to the Persian Gulf.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Hadrian withdrew from Mesopotamia and fortified borders, Marcus Aurelius fought the Marcomanni, and Antoninus Pius ruled in peace.

questions.question: What is the name of the stone and turf defensive wall built in northern Britain in 122 CE on the emperor's order?
questions.explanation_correct: Hadrian's Wall protected Roman Britain from Pictish raids coming from today's Scotland.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Antonine Wall was built later further north, Limes were fortifications on the Rhine and Danube, and Trajan's Wall was in Dacia.

questions.question: Which emperor, known as the 'philosopher on the throne', wrote the 'Meditations' and spent his reign fighting wars on the Danube?
questions.explanation_correct: Marcus Aurelius was a Stoic philosopher, and his notes were written during campaigns against the Quadi and Marcomanni.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Verus was co-emperor, Commodus was his son who fought as a gladiator, and Hadrian was a master administrator.

questions.question: Which emperor instituted the tetrarchy reform, dividing imperial power between two Augusti and two Caesars?
questions.explanation_correct: Diocletian (reigned 284–305 CE) established the Dominate, ending the Third Century Crisis and decentralizing administration.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Constantine reunified the empire, Aurelian unified it after secessions, and Severus founded a military dynasty.

questions.question: Which Roman emperor issued the Edict of Milan in 313 CE, granting religious freedom to Christians?
questions.explanation_correct: Constantine the Great was baptized on his deathbed and moved the capital to Constantinople.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Theodosius made Christianity the state religion, Julian tried to restore paganism, and Decius persecuted Christians.

questions.question: Which emperor made Christianity the state religion of Rome in 380 CE and banned the Olympic Games?
questions.explanation_correct: Theodosius's Edict of Thessalonica made Nicene Christianity the sole legal religion, banning pagan cults.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Constantine granted tolerance, and Arcadius and Honorius were his sons who inherited the divided empire.

questions.question: In which year did the final division of the Roman Empire into Western and Eastern halves occur after Theodosius's death?
questions.explanation_correct: In 395, Theodosius divided the empire between his sons: Honorius (West) and Arcadius (East).
questions.explanation_incorrect: 476 was the fall of the West, 330 was the founding of Constantinople, and 410 was the sack of Rome by the Visigoths.

questions.question: Which King of the Visigoths captured and sacked Rome in 410 CE, shocking the ancient world?
questions.explanation_correct: Alaric's sack of Rome was the first time the city fell to a foreign enemy in 800 years.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Odoacer deposed the last emperor, Genseric sacked Rome in 455 as King of the Vandals, and Attila was the Hun leader.

questions.question: Which Germanic chieftain deposed the last Western Roman Emperor, Romulus Augustulus, in 476 CE?
questions.explanation_correct: Odoacer sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople and declared himself King of Italy, marking the end of antiquity.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Theodoric founded the Ostrogothic Kingdom in Italy, Alaric took Rome in 410, and Geiseric (Genseric) was the Vandal chief.

questions.question: Which 3rd-century Roman emperor, styled 'Restitutor Orbis', reunified the empire by recovering Gaul and Palmyra?
questions.explanation_correct: Aurelian defeated Zenobia of Palmyra and recovered the Gallic Empire, also building a giant wall around Rome.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Gallienus defended borders, Caracalla granted citizenship to free men, and Valerian was captured by the Persians.

questions.question: What was the name of the first written code of Roman law from the 5th century BCE, displayed in the Forum?
questions.explanation_correct: The Law of the Twelve Tables (Lex Duodecim Tabularum) was the foundation of Roman public and private law.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Code of Justinian was compiled in the 6th century CE in Byzantium, and the praetorian edict was issued annually.

questions.question: Which temple to all gods in Rome, commissioned by Agrippa and rebuilt by Hadrian, features a dome with an oculus?
questions.explanation_correct: The Pantheon survived intact because it was converted into a Christian church in the 7th century.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Temple of Jupiter was destroyed, Vesta's temple was small and round, and Maxentius's basilica served as a law court.

questions.question: What was the name of the stone channels that transported fresh water from mountain springs to Roman cities?
questions.explanation_correct: Roman aqueducts relied entirely on gravity, requiring a precise, constant slope to transport water.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Viae were roads, Thermae were baths, and Cloacae were sewer systems.

questions.question: Which road, connecting Rome to Brindisi, was the oldest and most important, called the 'Queen of Roads'?
questions.explanation_correct: Construction of the Appian Way (Via Appia) was begun by censor Appius Claudius Caecus in 312 BCE during the Samnite Wars.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Flaminian Way led north, the Salarian Way was for salt transport, and the Aurelian Way ran along the Tuscan coast.

questions.question: Who were the priestesses who guarded the sacred fire of Rome, bound to a vow of chastity?
questions.explanation_correct: Vestals enjoyed immense respect and legal privileges, but breaking their vow was punished by burial alive.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Sibyls were prophetesses, haruspices read animal entrails, and augurs read bird flights.

questions.question: Which Roman poet wrote the national epic 'Aeneid', describing the flight of Aeneas from Troy to Italy?
questions.explanation_correct: Virgil wrote the 'Aeneid' commissioned by Augustus to legitimize the new ruling dynasty.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Horace wrote Odes, Ovid wrote Metamorphoses, and Juvenal wrote satires.

questions.question: What was the central public space in Rome used for elections, speeches, and trials, located between the hills?
questions.explanation_correct: The Forum Romanum was the political heart of the republic, adorned with temples, triumphal arches, and the rostra speaking platform.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Campus Martius was for military exercises, Capitoline was the temple hill, and Palatine held imperial palaces.

questions.question: Which general reformed the Roman army by creating a professional force, recruiting landless citizens?
questions.explanation_correct: Marius's reforms created legionaries loyal to their general rather than the state, easing the rise of civil wars.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Sulla was his rival and dictator, Pompey conquered Syria, and Crassus suppressed Spartacus.

questions.question: What were the lists issued by Sulla after capturing Rome containing names of outlawed enemies to be executed?
questions.explanation_correct: Anyone could kill a proscribed person on the lists for a reward, and the victim's property was confiscated.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Edicts were official decrees, censor tables were wealth records, and Roman statutes were general laws.

questions.question: Which war from 264–241 BCE, fought mainly over Sicily and at sea, began the rivalry between Rome and Carthage?
questions.explanation_correct: The First Punic War ended with Rome gaining Sicily, Sardinia, and Corsica – its first overseas provinces.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Second Punic War involved Hannibal, the Third destroyed Carthage, and the Macedonian War conquered Greece.

questions.question: At which battle in 48 BCE did Julius Caesar defeat Pompey's forces, forcing him to flee to Egypt?
questions.explanation_correct: The Battle of Pharsalus in Thessaly was the decisive land engagement of Caesar's civil war against the Senate.
questions.explanation_incorrect: At Thapsus and Munda Caesar defeated Pompey's remaining loyalists, and Actium was fought by Octavian.

questions.question: Which emperor was nicknamed 'Caligula' (Little Boot) because he wore small military boots as a child in Rhine camps?
questions.explanation_correct: Caligula hated his nickname as emperor. In history, he was recorded as a tyrannical and unstable ruler.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Claudius was his uncle, Tiberius his adopted grandfather, and Nero his nephew.

questions.question: Which stuttering emperor, considered weak in his youth, ruled wisely from 41 CE and annexed Britain?
questions.explanation_correct: Claudius reorganized administration, built the port of Ostia, and was likely poisoned by his wife Agrippina.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Caligula was killed by the Praetorians, Vespasian took power after civil war, and Nero committed suicide.

questions.question: What was the turbulent period of civil war after Nero's death in 68 CE, ended by Wespasians's triumph?
questions.explanation_correct: In one year, Galba, Otho, Vitellius, and the final victor Vespasian fought for the throne.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Third Century Crisis lasted 50 years, the tetrarchy was a rule of four, and the Second Triumvirate was before the empire.

questions.question: Which two Roman towns were completely buried by ash after the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE?
questions.explanation_correct: The eruption of Vesuvius preserved the towns under ash, giving modern archaeologists priceless insights.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Naples and Capua survived, Syracuse is in Sicily, and Bari and Brindisi are in Apulia.

questions.question: Which emperor, Trajan's adopted son, ended conquests in the east and focused on fortifying empire borders (limes)?
questions.explanation_correct: Hadrian spent his reign traveling provinces, inspecting legions, and building fortifications.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Trajan was a conqueror, Antoninus ruled from Italy, and Marcus Aurelius returned to defensive wars.

questions.question: Which emperor issued the edict in 212 CE (Constitutio Antoniniana) granting citizenship to all free residents of the empire?
questions.explanation_correct: Caracalla issued the edict mainly to increase inheritance tax revenues, which only citizens paid.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Septimius was his father, Elagabalus his eccentric cousin, and Alexander the last of the Severans.

questions.question: What is the 50-year period of military anarchy and barbarian invasions in 235–284 CE, ended by Diocletian?
questions.explanation_correct: During this period, emperors were constantly overthrown by military usurpers, and the empire temporarily split into three.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tetrarchy resolved the crisis, the Dominate was the new system, and the Migration Period occurred in the 4th-5th centuries.

questions.question: Which emperor reunified the empire and founded the new capital on the Bosporus in 330 CE?
questions.explanation_correct: New Rome, later named Constantinople (former Byzantium), became the heart of the empire for another thousand years.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Diocletian introduced the tetrarchy, Theodosius divided the empire, and Julian ruled briefly.

questions.question: Which emperor, Constantine's nephew, made a failed attempt to restore paganism, earning the epithet 'Apostate'?
questions.explanation_correct: Julian revoked privileges for the Church and wrote anti-Christian treatises, but died in Persia in 363 CE.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Jovian restored Christianity, Valentinian ruled in the west, and Valens died at Adrianople.

questions.question: At which battle in 378 CE were Roman legions crushed by the Visigoths, resulting in the death of Emperor Valens?
questions.explanation_correct: The defeat at Adrianople showed the weakness of Roman infantry against barbarian cavalry.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Catalaunian Plains was fought against Attila (451 CE), Cannae was in the Punic War, and Actium was a civil war.

questions.question: Which Roman general of barbarian descent halted Attila the Hun's invasion at the Catalaunian Plains in 451 CE?
questions.explanation_correct: Flavius Aetius, called 'the last of the Romans', allied with the Visigoths to repel the Huns in Gaul.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Stilicho defended Rome in the early 5th century, Ricimer was a kingmaker general, and Bonifacius was Aetius's rival.

questions.question: Which Roman historian of the Augustan era wrote the monumental history 'Ab Urbe condita' (From the Founding of the City)?
questions.explanation_correct: Livy's work originally comprised 142 books, of which only 35 survive today.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tacitus wrote the Annals, Suetonius wrote the Lives of the Twelve Caesars, and Sallust wrote about the Jugurthine War.

questions.question: Which Roman biographer wrote the intimate details of the first twelve emperors in 'The Twelve Caesars'?
questions.explanation_correct: Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus, as secretary to Hadrian, had access to the imperial archives.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tacitus wrote critical histories, Livy focused on the republic, and Pliny described Vesuvius's eruption.

questions.question: What type of Roman clay vessel was used to transport wine, olive oil, and grain by sea?
questions.explanation_correct: Amphorae had pointed bottoms, allowing them to be packed tightly in ship holds.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Patera was a libation bowl, kantharos a wine cup, and rhyton a horn-like drinking vessel.

questions.question: Which was the largest imperial forum in Rome, featuring a column depicting the Dacian Wars?
questions.explanation_correct: The Forum of Trajan was the largest and grandest, designed by architect Apollodorus of Damascus.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Caesar's was first, Augustus's featured Mars Ultor, and Vespasian's held the Temple of Peace.

questions.question: What was the name for a Roman public bathhouse, serving as a center of social life, sports, and hygiene?
questions.explanation_correct: Thermae (like Caracalla or Diocletian) offered cold, warm, and hot pools, libraries, and gyms.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Curia was the senate house, basilica a law and trade hall, and insula an apartment building.

questions.question: What was the name of the great Roman circus used for chariot races, seating up to 250,000 spectators?
questions.explanation_correct: The Circus Maximus lay between the Palatine and Aventine hills and was Rome's oldest venue.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Colosseum was for gladiators, Pompey's was a theatre, and Domitian's stadium is today's Piazza Navona.

questions.question: Which of Rome's hills was the home of wealthy patricians and later the site of imperial palaces?
questions.explanation_correct: The name of the Palatine Hill is the origin of the word 'palace' (palatium) in European languages.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Capitoline was the temple hill, Aventine plebeian, and Esquiline residential.

questions.question: Which King of Pontus fought Rome in three wars and immunized himself to poisons by taking small doses?
questions.explanation_correct: Mithridates was defeated by Pompey and committed suicide by sword when poison failed to work.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tigranes ruled Armenia, Jugurtha was a Numidian king, and Ariovistus was a Germanic chief.

questions.question: Which Roman politician exposed and crushed the Catiline Conspiracy in 63 BCE, earning the title Father of the Fatherland?
questions.explanation_correct: Marcus Tullius Cicero delivered four speeches against Catiline, starting with 'Quousque tandem abutere...'.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Cato supported Cicero, Caesar opposed execution without trial, and Brutus was a young senator.

questions.question: Which two tribune brothers attempted to pass land reforms in the 2nd century BCE and were murdered by patricians?
questions.explanation_correct: Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus wanted to redistribute public land to poor citizens, meeting violent senatorial opposition.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Scipios were commanders, Brutus's were conspirators, and Decius's sacrificed themselves in battle.

questions.question: In which year BCE was the last Roman king Tarquin the Proud expelled and the Republic established?
questions.explanation_correct: The Republic was established after the rape of Lucretia by the king's son sparked a rebellion.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 753 BCE was Rome's founding, 390 BCE was the Gallic sack, and 27 BCE was the empire's start.

questions.question: Which Celtic tribe under Brennus captured and burned Rome around 390 BCE, demanding a ransom in gold?
questions.explanation_correct: This invasion led to the legend of the Capitoline geese and Brennus's phrase 'Vae victis' (Woe to the vanquished).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Vandals and Visigoths sacked Rome in the 5th century CE, and Germans is a general group.

questions.question: Which legendary Roman patrician left his plow in 458 BCE to become dictator, defeated enemies in 16 days, and resigned?
questions.explanation_correct: Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus became the Roman symbol of civic virtue and modesty.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Camillus saved Rome from Gauls, Fabius fought Hannibal, and Coriolanus fought the Volscians.

questions.question: With which kingdom in Asia Minor did Rome fight three wars under Sulla, Lucullus, and Pompey?
questions.explanation_correct: The Mithridatic Wars ended with the annexation of Pontus and the reorganization of the Roman East.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Parthia was a Mesopotamian rival, Armenia allied with Pontus, and Egypt was annexed in 30 BCE.

questions.question: Which King of Epirus invaded Italy in the 3rd century BCE, winning victories at such high cost that it spawned a saying?
questions.explanation_correct: Pyrrhus's victory at Asculum (279 BCE) led him to say: 'If we are victorious in one more battle, we shall be ruined'.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Alexander I ruled Macedon, Mithridates ruled Pontus, and Antiochus III ruled Syria.

questions.question: What was the title of the Roman magistrate appointed only during emergencies for a maximum of six months?
questions.explanation_correct: A dictator held absolute power (imperium maius) and was not subject to tribunician veto.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Consul was a yearly office, praetor ran courts, and censor conducted the census.

questions.question: Which Roman magistrate was responsible for courts and had the right to lead armies in the consul's absence?
questions.explanation_correct: Praetors ran trials, issued annual edicts setting legal rules, and could govern smaller provinces.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Aediles oversaw city order, quaestors managed treasury, and tribunes represented plebeians.

questions.question: Which Roman magistrate controlled state finances, managed the treasury in the Temple of Saturn, and served as military treasurer?
questions.explanation_correct: The quaestorship was the first rung on the Roman career path (cursus honorum), giving entry to the Senate.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Aediles organized games, praetors were judges, and censors ran the census.

questions.question: Which Roman magistrate was responsible for public roads, grain supply, and organizing games at their own expense?
questions.explanation_correct: Aediles built popularity by funding games, which helped them get elected as consuls later.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Quaestors managed funds, praetors courts, and censors the census.

questions.question: How many censors were elected by the Roman Senate once every five years, usually from ex-consuls, for 18 months?
questions.explanation_correct: Two censors conducted the census, assessed wealth, and could remove senators for immoral behavior (nota censoria).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Roman collegiate offices usually had two or multiples of two magistrates.

questions.question: Which Roman magistrate held veto rights against other magistrates and personal sacrosanctity?
questions.explanation_correct: Tribunes of the Plebs were elected by plebeians to protect them from patrician abuses.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Consuls and praetors were subject to veto, and censors were excluded in census matters.

questions.question: What was the term for the sequential order of public offices held by aspiring politicians in the Roman Republic?
questions.explanation_correct: The cursus honorum required serving as quaestor, aedile (optional), praetor, and finally consul.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Pax Romana was the Roman peace, mos maiorum was ancestral custom, and pomerium was Rome's sacred boundary.

questions.question: What was the sacred boundary of the city of Rome, within which carrying weapons or commanding troops was forbidden?
questions.explanation_correct: Crossing the pomerium with troops without Senate approval was treason, broken by Julius Caesar.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Limes was the state border, cardo the north-south street, and decumanus the east-west street.

questions.question: Which dynasty, founded by Augustus, ruled Rome until Nero's suicide in 68 CE?
questions.explanation_correct: This dynasty united the Julian (from Caesar) and Claudian (from Livia, Augustus's wife) families.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Flavians ruled after Nero, Antonines in the 2nd century, and Severans in the late 2nd to early 3rd century.

questions.question: Which emperor, Augustus's successor, spent his final years on Capri, leaving Rome to Praetorian Prefect Sejanus?
questions.explanation_correct: Tiberius was a military commander but grew suspicious as emperor, withdrawing from Rome.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Caligula ruled from Palatine palaces, Claudius ruled with freedmen, and Nero focused on art.

questions.question: Which emperor, Vespasian's son, captured and destroyed Jerusalem in 70 CE, suppressing the Jewish Revolt?
questions.explanation_correct: Titus built a triumphal arch in Rome commemorating the Temple's destruction and the capture of the menorah.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Domitian was his brother, Nero started the war by sending Vespasian, and Trajan conquered Dacia.

questions.question: What was the period of relative peace and stability in the empire during the 1st and 2nd centuries CE, started by Augustus?
questions.explanation_correct: Pax Romana allowed trade to flourish, roads to be built, and provinces to be Romanized.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tetrarchy was a rule of four, and Principate was the name of the early empire's political system.

questions.question: Which emperor erected a monumental column in Rome showing his victories in the Dacian Wars in spiral reliefs?
questions.explanation_correct: Trajan's Column stands in his forum and served as his tomb (his ashes were placed in its base).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Marcus Aurelius's column shows Germanic wars, and Hadrian and Antoninus built no such columns.

questions.question: Which Roman emperor was the first to be killed in battle against a foreign enemy, defeated by Goths at Abrittus in 251 CE?
questions.explanation_correct: Emperor Decius and his son Herennius died in marshes at Abrittus fighting the Goths under Kniva.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Valerian was captured by Persians, Aurelian was assassinated by officers, and Gallienus died in a coup.

questions.question: Which Roman emperor was captured by Persian King Shapur I in 260 CE and died in captivity?
questions.explanation_correct: The Persian war ended in humiliation – Shapur allegedly used Valerian as a mounting block for his horse.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Decius died at Abrittus, Gallienus was Valerian's son, and Aurelian rebuilt the empire.

questions.question: What was the breakaway state in Gaul and Britain that split from Rome during the Third Century Crisis?
questions.explanation_correct: The Gallic Empire (Imperium Galliarum) was founded by Postumus in 260 and lasted until Aurelian's conquest in 274.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Palmyra was an eastern breakaway state, Britain was part of Gaul's empire, and Dacia was abandoned.

questions.question: What was the eastern state ruled by Queen Zenobia that took control of Egypt and Syria in the 3rd century CE?
questions.explanation_correct: Zenobia declared independence, but her empire was destroyed by Emperor Aurelian in 272 CE.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Gallic Empire was in the west, Parthians were eastern rivals, and Nabataea was annexed by Trajan.

questions.question: Which emperor founded the Severan dynasty in 193 CE, basing his rule on military force?
questions.explanation_correct: Severus advised his sons on his deathbed: 'Be harmonious, enrich the soldiers, and scorn all others'.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Caracalla was his son, Pertinax was killed by Praetorians, and Julianus bought the throne at auction.

questions.question: Which eccentric Severan emperor tried to make the Syrian sun god Elagabal the supreme deity of Rome?
questions.explanation_correct: Elagabalus shocked Romans with orgies, marrying a Vestal Virgin, and Eastern religious rites.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Caracalla was brutal, Alexander was tolerant, and Geta was killed by Caracalla.

questions.question: Which Roman imperial system, introduced by Diocletian, replaced the Principate and featured absolute rule?
questions.explanation_correct: The name Dominate comes from 'dominus' (lord/master), reflecting the emperor's shift to an absolute ruler.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tetrarchy was a rule of four within the Dominate, Principate was Augustus's system, and autocracy is a general term.

questions.question: Which Roman emperor ordered the construction of a massive defensive wall around Rome in the 270s CE?
questions.explanation_correct: The 19 km Aurelian Walls were built to protect Rome from Germanic invasions during the crisis.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Probus continued works, Diocletian moved provincial capitals, and Marcus Aurelius built northern walls.

questions.question: Which Roman province, covering today's Egypt, was called the 'granary of Rome' and served as the emperor's private domain?
questions.explanation_correct: Egypt supplied grain for Rome's free distribution (annona), and senators needed permission to enter.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Cyrenaica lay west of Egypt, Syria was a border province, and Africa Proconsularis was in Tunisia.

questions.question: Which King of the Vandals sacked Rome in 455 CE, looting treasures and carrying them to Carthage?
questions.explanation_correct: The Vandal sack under Genseric lasted 14 days and permanently impoverished Rome, inspiring the term 'vandalism'.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Alaric took Rome in 410, Attila withdrew after meeting Pope Leo I, and Theodoric ruled Italy later.

questions.question: Which Pope met Attila the Hun in 452 CE, persuading him to abandon his march on Rome?
questions.explanation_correct: Leo I saved Rome from the Huns and in 455 negotiated with Vandal king Genseric to spare citizens' lives.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Gregory I lived in the 6th century, Sylvester I served under Constantine, and Gelasius formulated the two-swords theory.

questions.question: What was the most common Roman silver coin, serving as the basic currency unit?
questions.explanation_correct: The denarius originally contained about 4.5 grams of pure silver, though it debased heavily over time.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Sestertius was brass, as was copper, and aureus was gold.

questions.question: What was the Roman gold coin introduced in the late Republic, valued at 25 denarii?
questions.explanation_correct: The aureus was used for large transactions and payouts to high-ranking army officers.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The solidus replaced the aureus in the 4th century under Constantine.

questions.question: Which Roman architect and engineer of the 1st century BCE wrote the treaty 'De architectura'?
questions.explanation_correct: Vitruvius described human body proportions that later inspired Leonardo da Vinci's 'Vitruvian Man'.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Apollodorus built Trajan's forum, Frontinus described aqueducts, and Pliny wrote the natural history.

questions.question: Which Roman senator wrote 'De aquaeductu' in the 1st century CE, describing Rome's aqueduct system?
questions.explanation_correct: Sextus Julius Frontinus, as curator aquarum, targeted illegal water tapping by private owners.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Vitruvius wrote about architecture generally, Pliny about natural history, and Agrippa built the first imperial aqueducts.

questions.question: What was the name of the bronze or iron scraper used to clean oil and sweat from the skin in bathhouses?
questions.explanation_correct: Romans did not use soap; they rubbed themselves with olive oil and scraped it off with a strigil.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Patera was a bowl, aryballos a Greek oil jar, and ampulla a small flask.

questions.question: Which woolen garment could only be worn by free male Roman citizens?
questions.explanation_correct: The toga was official and uncomfortable; slaves and foreigners were banned from wearing it.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The tunica was daily wear for all, the stola was a married woman's dress, and the palla was a female cloak.

questions.question: What was the title of the male head of a Roman household, holding absolute legal power (patria potestas)?
questions.explanation_correct: The pater familias decided on life, death, marriages, and managed family property.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Patron was a client protector, plebeian a lower-class citizen, and patrician an aristocrat.

questions.question: Which Roman Stoic philosopher, dramatist, and tutor to Nero was forced by him to commit suicide?
questions.explanation_correct: Seneca wrote 'Moral Letters to Lucilius' and opened his veins after being accused of joining the Pisonian conspiracy.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Epictetus was a 2nd-century freedman Stoic, Cicero an eclectic, and Lucretius an Epicurean.

questions.question: What is the famous philosophical poem by Lucretius, popularizing Epicurean materialism in Rome?
questions.explanation_correct: The poem 'De rerum natura' explained the world through atomist physics, freeing humans from fear of gods and death.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Meditations was by Marcus Aurelius, The Art of Love by Ovid, and Satires by Juvenal.

questions.question: Which Roman historian wrote the 'Annals', covering the Julio-Claudian dynasty from Tiberius to Nero?
questions.explanation_correct: Tacitus wrote 'sine ira et studio' (without anger and fondness), criticizing the empire's moral decline.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Suetonius wrote biographies, Livy wrote about the Republic, and Cassius Dio wrote in Greek in the 3rd century.

questions.question: Which 1st-century CE writer compiled the first encyclopedia 'Natural History' and died in the Vesuvius eruption?
questions.explanation_correct: Pliny the Elder compiled 20,000 facts on biology, geography, and art, dying while trying to rescue people at Stabiae.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Pliny the Younger was his nephew, who described his uncle's death in letters to Tacitus.

questions.question: What was the name of the multi-story apartment buildings inhabited by poorer Roman classes?
questions.explanation_correct: Insulae were often built cheaply of wood and mud brick, collapsing or burning down frequently.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Domus was a private town house, villa a country estate, and atrium a courtyard.

questions.question: What was the name of the private town house of a wealthy Roman family?
questions.explanation_correct: A domus was closed off to the street, with rooms centered around an atrium and peristyle.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Insula was an apartment block, villa a country estate, and taberna a shop or inn.

questions.question: What was the central, open courtyard of a Roman house, where rainwater collected in the impluvium pool?
questions.explanation_correct: The atrium was the heart of the house, where guests were received and family shrine images (lararium) kept.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Peristyle was a colonnaded garden, tablinum the office, and triclinium the dining room.

questions.question: What was the Roman dining room with three couches arranged around a low table for dining reclining?
questions.explanation_correct: Diners reclined on their left side, which was the proper dining posture during formal banquets.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tablinum was the study, atrium the courtyard, and culina the kitchen.

questions.question: Which Roman general suppressed the Spartacus rebellion in 71 BCE and crucified 6,000 slaves along the Appian Way?
questions.explanation_correct: Marcus Crassus was the richest man in Rome, and defeating Spartacus was meant to bring him military fame.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Pompey took credit for clearing the remnants, Lucullus fought in Asia, and Caesar was a military tribune.

questions.question: Which Roman general conquered Gaul in 58–50 BCE, describing the campaign in 'Commentarii de Bello Gallico'?
questions.explanation_correct: Conquering Gaul gave Caesar the loyalty of veterans and the wealth needed to take power.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Pompey was in Rome, Antony was Caesar's officer, and Augustus was a child.

questions.question: Which King of the Arverni unified Gallic tribes against Caesar and was defeated at Alesia in 52 BCE?
questions.explanation_correct: Vercingetorix surrendered at Alesia, was imprisoned in Rome, and executed after Caesar's triumph.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Dumnorix and Orgetorix were other Gallic leaders, and Ambiorix led the Eburones.

questions.question: Which mountain tribe of central Italy fought Rome in three wars for dominion in the 4th and 3rd centuries BCE?
questions.explanation_correct: The Samnite Wars led to the humilating Roman defeat at the Caudine Forks in 321 BCE.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Etruscans lived to the north, Latins were close neighbors, and Sabines integrated with early Rome.

questions.question: In which mountain pass in 321 BCE did the Samnites surround Roman legions, forcing them under a yoke?
questions.explanation_correct: The defeat at the Caudine Forks (Furculae Caudinae) was a major stain on Roman military honor.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Brenner is in the Alps, Thermopylae in Greece, and Karkonosze in Poland.

questions.question: Which northern Italian tribe influenced early Rome, providing its last three kings and its alphabet?
questions.explanation_correct: Etruscans passed on arch construction, augury, and symbols of power like the fasces bundle.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Samnites lived east, Ligurians west, and Gauls invaded Rome later.

questions.question: Which mythical Trojan hero, who fled destroyed Troy, is considered the ancestor of the Romans in Italy?
questions.explanation_correct: Aeneas reached Latium and founded Lavinium, starting the royal line of Alba Longa.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Romulus was his descendant living centuries later, Priam was Troy's king, and Hector Troy's defender.

questions.question: What was the name of the highest, privileged social class holding a monopoly on offices in early Rome?
questions.explanation_correct: Patricians descended from Rome's oldest families and held seats in the early Senate.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Plebeians were the rest of the citizens, equites were the middle class, and nobiles were late-republican ruling elites.

questions.question: What was the free but initially politically powerless social class in Rome that fought for rights against patricians?
questions.explanation_correct: Plebeians (plebs) won the office of tribune and written laws by using general strikes (secessions).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Patricians were the ruling class, equites were rich merchants, and slaves had no freedom.

questions.question: In which year BCE did the Romans destroy Carthage, ending the Third Punic War?
questions.explanation_correct: In the same year 146 BCE, Romans destroyed Corinth, completing the conquest of Greece.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 202 BCE was the Battle of Zama, 133 BCE was Tiberius Gracchus's death, and 44 BCE was Caesar's death.

questions.question: Which general and son-in-law of Augustus built the first Pantheon and organized aqueducts and the empire map?
questions.explanation_correct: Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa was Augustus's closest friend and a brilliant military commander (won Actium).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Antony was Augustus's enemy, Maecenas was a patron of art, and Tiberius succeeded Augustus.

questions.question: What term is used for a rich patron of the arts, named after Augustus's advisor who supported Horace and Virgil?
questions.explanation_correct: Gaius Cilnius Maecenas established a literary circle supporting the cultural policy of the new empire.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Patron is a general term, and Augustus and Princeps are imperial titles.

questions.question: What was the provincial capital of Roman Dacia, founded by Trajan in the Carpathian Mountains?
questions.explanation_correct: The city was founded near the former Dacian capital destroyed in Trajan's wars against Decebalus.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Apulum and Napoca were smaller Dacian towns, and Singidunum is today's Belgrade.

questions.question: Which King of Dacia fought Trajan and committed suicide in 106 CE to avoid capture?
questions.explanation_correct: Decebalus unified Dacia; the gold spoils captured from his kingdom rescued Roman state finances.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Burebista ruled a century earlier, Tigranes was King of Armenia, and Vercingetorix led the Gauls.

questions.question: Which 2nd-century CE writer coined the phrase 'Panem et circenses' (Bread and circuses), criticizing the passive plebs?
questions.explanation_correct: Juvenal, in his Satires, lamented that the mob that once gave out legions now only wants free grain and races.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Horace wrote lyrics, Virgil wrote the epic, and Petronius wrote the Satyricon.

questions.question: Which famous Roman novel, attributed to Petronius, features a satire on Nero's society and the banquet of Trimalchio?
questions.explanation_correct: Only fragments of the Satyricon survive, portraying the lives of wealthy freedmen in a critical light.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Metamorphoses was by Ovid, The Golden Ass by Apuleius, and Pharsalia by Lucan.

questions.question: Which 2nd-century CE writer wrote 'The Golden Ass' (Metamorphoses), the only Latin novel to survive in its entirety?
questions.explanation_correct: Apuleius of Madaura wrote about Lucius, who is accidentally turned into an ass, including the myth of Cupid and Psyche.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Petronius's Satyricon is only fragmentary, Juvenal wrote satires, and Pliny wrote letters.

questions.question: What was the solemn entry of a victorious commander into Rome, approved by the Senate, where the general painted his face red?
questions.explanation_correct: During a triumph, the general rode a chariot as Jupiter's incarnation, while a slave whispered 'Memento mori'.
questions.explanation_incorrect: An ovation was a lesser triumph on foot, salute is a greeting, and adventus is the emperor's arrival.

questions.question: What was the lesser award for victory in the Roman military, given when a war was not fully formal?
questions.explanation_correct: During an ovation (ovatio), the general walked or rode a horse and sacrificed a sheep (ovis) instead of bulls.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A triumph was the highest award, phalerae were chest medals, and the laurel wreath was a general symbol.

questions.question: Who was the chief priest of Rome, heading the College of Pontiffs and overseeing state religion?
questions.explanation_correct: Augustus assumed the title of Pontifex Maximus, worn by all subsequent emperors and now the Pope.
questions.explanation_incorrect: A flamen was dedicated to a specific deity, an augur read flights, and sacerdos is the general word for priest.

questions.question: What was the name for the household spirits guarding the home, family, and pantry?
questions.explanation_correct: Lares guarded estate boundaries and the house, while Penates looked after the pantry and food supply.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Manes were ancestral spirits, lemures were malevolent night ghosts, and genii were male life forces.

questions.question: What were the ancestral spirits worshipped as protective deities during the Parentalia festival?
questions.explanation_correct: Romans built altars and gravestones with the inscription D.M. (Dis Manibus - To the Divine Manes).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Lemures were ghosts of the unburied, lares guarded homes, and genii were life forces.

questions.question: What was the festival honoring Saturn in December, during which slaves and masters exchanged roles?
questions.explanation_correct: During Saturnalia work was banned, and people gave each other candles and clay figures.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Lupercalia was in February, Compitalia honored crossroad shrines, and Vulcanalia honored Vulcan in August.

questions.question: What was the purification and fertility festival in February where priests ran around the Palatine striking women with goat-skin straps?
questions.explanation_correct: Lupercalia was associated with the she-wolf that nursed Romulus, aiming to grant women fertility.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Saturnalia was in December, Liberalia in March for wine and freedom, and Cerealia for Ceres in April.
